Computer-use agents bring this promise within reach by capably executing fully specified tasks across apps. However, real-world user requests are often underspecified. To act correctly for the particular user, an agent must infer some missing information from the user’s activity history and ask for other information that only the user can provide, without making unsupported assumptions or burdening the user with unnecessary questions. We present iPrefBench, a benchmark for evaluating the infer and ask capabilities of personal mobile-use agents in an executable iOS environment with an interactive simulated user. Grounded in a coherent persona with 3 , 051 3,051 past activity events, iPrefBench comprises 130 130 underspecified user tasks across 26 26 apps. Each omitted user-dependent requirement is, by construction, either history-inferable or ask-only. iPrefBench evaluates personalized mobile agents on both whether agents complete tasks correctly for the user (i.e., personalized task completion) and whether they seek user input when necessary (i.e., user-agent interaction). Evaluation of 7 7 frontier agents reveals a substantial gap between execution and personalization. Agents achieve high action completion scores (up to 91.6 91.6 %) but low full task success (up to 47.7 47.7 %) because personalization lags behind. They especially struggle with ask-only information, failing to request enough necessary information. Our findings highlight a challenge for personalized agents in knowing what to infer and when to ask. We hope that iPrefBench can serve as a valuable testbed for building agents that know their user and work with them. 1 Introduction It has been a long-standing goal in Artificial Intelligence and Human-Computer Interaction to develop agents that can understand and act on behalf of users ( Maes and Kozierok, 1993 ; Lieberman, 1997 ; Horvitz, 1999 ) . Recent computer-use agents (CUAs) have made rapid progress in completing digital tasks across apps and over long horizons ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Rawles et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2025 ) . These agents often excel at fully specified tasks (e.g., “make a reservation at Harborline Seafood tomorrow at 7:30 PM for a party of four.”). However, realistic user queries rarely provide complete details, and are often underspecified ( Völkel et al., 2021 ) . For example, a user may say “book me my usual restaurant for tomorrow” instead of specifying the restaurant name, reservation time, and party size. Figure 1 : iPrefBench evaluates personalized mobile-use agents on underspecified user tasks that require both inferring user-specific information from grounded activity history and asking the user for information unavailable from history. Contending with such underspecified tasks requires personalization capabilities, in which an agent resolves missing information in two ways: infer from knowledge of the user (e.g., the user’s usual restaurant from past reservations and orders), and ask for details that the available history does not establish (e.g., the desired time and party size). An agent that silently makes unsupported assumptions can diverge from a user’s actual intent, while an agent that asks for details already inferable from the user’s history defeats the purpose of autonomy. A truly useful personal agent must reason not only about what information is missing, but also where it should come from. Yet this challenge is not fully captured by existing evaluations. Typical CUA benchmarks fully specify every task and cold-start agents without any knowledge of the user ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Rawles et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) , leaving nothing to infer or ask. Benchmarks with underspecified tasks usually supply only one resolution source: personalization benchmarks expose a user history but offer no one to ask ( Lyu et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , while interactive benchmarks provide a simulated user but no user history that would make some questions unnecessary ( Yao et al., 2024 ; Vijayvargiya et al., 2026 ) . Some provide both ( Chen et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026c ) , but do not distinguish which missing details should be inferred and which require clarification. Therefore, they cannot measure whether the agent knows what to infer and when to ask. To bridge the gap, we present iPrefBench, a benchmark designed around the infer-and-ask capabilities of personalized mobile-use agents in an executable iOS environment. As shown in Figure 1 , agents can know about the user through two sources: an activity history, provided as their only prior context, and a simulated user, reachable through an ask_user action, who answers clarification questions. Both are grounded in rich seeded data around one coherent persona in the environment. iPrefBench comprises 130 130 underspecified tasks, and each omitted detail is designed to be either inferable (i.e., grounded in specific evidence in activity history) or ask-only (i.e., held solely by the simulated user). To further assess whether agents can apply historical preferences appropriately in challenging real-world scenarios, we include tasks in which current instructions override past patterns, recent behavior indicates changing preferences, or preferred options are unavailable. iPrefBench assesses both whether agents complete tasks correctly for the user (i.e., personalized task completion ) and whether they seek user input when necessary (i.e., user-agent interaction ). Personalized task completion is measured by task-specific rubrics, split into two types: action-completion criteria measure whether required operations were successfully executed (e.g., a restaurant reservation was made), while personalization criteria measure whether each user-dependent decision matches the intended values (e.g., the restaurant, time, and party size). However, correct outcomes alone do not establish user satisfaction: an agent may succeed by interrogating the user about every detail, or luckily guessing the ask-only information correctly. Therefore, inspired by Grice’s maxims ( Grice et al., 1975 ) , we also evaluate user-agent interaction through recall and precision on ask-only information: recall measures whether the agent elicits all required ask-only information, while precision measures whether its requests obtain new ask-only information rather than ask for inferable or irrelevant details or repeat earlier requests. We evaluate seven frontier agents on iPrefBench. The results reveal a substantial gap between executing a task successfully and personalizing it for a particular user. Although Claude Opus 5, the best-performing agent evaluated, achieves a 91.6 91.6 % action-completion score, its task success rate is only 47.7 47.7 % because personalization lags behind. Agents struggle particularly with ask-only information, and our interaction evaluation reveals a corresponding shortfall. By default, agents ask far too little: the recall on ask-only information is low across the board, with the highest at only 44.3 44.3 %. Yet what they do ask is not reliably necessary either, with precision between 60 60 % and 77 77 %. Explicitly adding a clarification phase can substantially increase the number of questions and raise the recall and task success rate, but lower precision in turn, exposing a tradeoff between silent guessing and excessive user burden. The challenge is therefore not simply to ask more, but to determine when asking is necessary. We hope iPrefBench can serve as a valuable testbed for building agents that know their user and work with them effectively. 2 Related Work Computer-Use Agent Benchmarks. Computer-use agents have advanced rapidly ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Hong et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) , supported by executable benchmarks across desktop ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) , mobile ( Rawles et al., 2025 ) , and web environments ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Koh et al., 2024 ; Xue et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2024 ) . These benchmarks typically use fully specified tasks without prior user knowledge. MobileWorld ( Kong et al., 2026 ) introduces underspecified tasks and an ask_user action, but without user history, every missing detail must be asked. Personalized Agent Benchmarks. A growing line of work evaluates preference inference from user histories for personalized tasks, but does not support interactive clarification ( Cai et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Lyu et al., 2026 ) . iOSWorld ( Jang et al., 2026 ) , on which our environment builds, seeds an iOS simulator with a coherent persona but neither exposes user history as prior context nor supports user interaction. VitaBench 2.0 ( Chen et al., 2026c ) and KnowU-Bench ( Chen et al., 2026b ) incorporate user histories and, in some cases, hidden information accessible through simulated users, but do not explicitly distinguish whether each missing detail is recoverable from the history or known only to the user, and thus cannot evaluate the efficiency of user-agent interaction, i.e., whether agents only ask necessary questions. Interactive and Clarification Benchmarks. Interactive benchmarks ( Yao et al., 2024 ; Qian et al., 2024 ; Qian et al., 2025 ; Barres et al., 2025 ; Vijayvargiya et al., 2026 ) study clarification with simulated users whom agents have no prior knowledge of, and mainly measure task outcomes or how much hidden information agents elicit. Ask-before-Plan ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) penalizes missed and unnecessary questions, while AppWorld-UL ( Chen et al., 2026a ) evaluates information elicitation under underspecification, infeasibility, and confirmation-seeking scenarios. However, all of these settings lack user histories against which the necessity of clarification questions can be assessed. In contrast, iPrefBench evaluates agents on underspecified tasks, whose missing information can either be inferred from grounded user history or only be obtained by asking the user, and explicitly distinguishes the resolution source, enabling evaluation of personalized task completion and necessity-aware user-agent interaction. We provide a detailed comparison in Table A.1 . 3 iPrefBench 3.1 Benchmark Overview iPrefBench evaluates whether mobile-use agents can complete underspecified tasks for a user, by inferring missing information from user history and seeking clarification when necessary. For each task t ∈ 𝒯 t\in\mathcal{T} , let U t U_{t} denote the user-dependent details left unresolved by the instruction. Each u ∈ U t u\in U_{t} has an intended value and exactly one resolution source: (1) Inferable information ( u ∈ U t infer u\in U_{t}^{\mathrm{infer}} ): Information whose intended value can be recovered from consistent evidence in the user activity history ℋ \mathcal{H} , such as a dominant pattern across past events or a stable user fact. (2) Ask-only information ( u ∈ U t ask u\in U_{t}^{\mathrm{ask}} ): Information unavailable in ℋ \mathcal{H} that must be obtained by asking the user, such as the context of the current occasion. This split mirrors what a personal assistant can know about its user: stable preferences and habits leave traces in past activity, whereas the specifics of the current situation do not. This distinction allows us to evaluate both whether agents infer user-specific details correctly from the history, and whether they seek clarification only when needed, without unnecessary questions. 3.2 Environment Executable iOS Environment. iPrefBench builds on the executable iOS simulator from iOSWorld ( Jang et al., 2026 ) , containing 26 26 mock apps populated with interconnected data (e.g., past restaurant reservations, financial transactions, messages, workouts and ticket orders) for a coherent user persona, Jordan Avery . The agent operates through standard mobile GUI actions (e.g., tap , type , and swipe ). We extend the action space with an ask_user action, which allows the agent to send a natural language message to the simulated user and receive a user response. Full details of the action space are provided in Appendix B.2 . User Activity History. We compose seeded application data as a chronological user activity history ℋ \mathcal{H} (Appendix C.1 ), representing a timeline of what the user did on their personal phone. Each event is converted from the underlying application metadata into natural-language descriptions. The activity history ℋ \mathcal{H} is provided to the agent as the only prior knowledge and context of the user. All inferable information (e.g., recurring preferences, habits and user facts) is designed to be recoverable from evidence in ℋ \mathcal{H} . User Profile and User Simulator. To ground simulated user responses and facilitate evaluation, we derive a structured user profile 𝒫 \mathcal{P} from the seeded application data (Appendix C.2 ), consolidating the persona’s preferences, habits, and personal information into 13 13 dimensions (e.g., identity, social relationships, finances, dining and travel preferences, and fitness habits). 𝒫 \mathcal{P} is hidden from the agent and serves as a ground-truth reference for user simulation and evaluation. We simulate the interactive user with an LLM grounded in 𝒫 \mathcal{P} and, when applicable, task-specific hidden context. When the agent issues an ask_user action, the user simulator answers the question in character. To faithfully evaluate the agent’s own ability to recognize what is missing, we instruct the simulator to answer only what is asked, without proactively volunteering additional information. 3.3 Tasks Task Design. As described in § 3.1 , each task intentionally leaves user-dependent details unspecified, with their intended values and resolution sources explicitly annotated. For example, “book me my usual restaurant for tomorrow” leaves three pieces of information underspecified: the restaurant, party size, and time. The user’s reservation history in ℋ \mathcal{H} can resolve the usual restaurant, so asking the user about it is redundant. In contrast, the reservation time and party size, which describe the current occasion and cannot be supported by any history, must be obtained by asking rather than assumed. A single task may contain multiple inferable and ask-only requirements, and often requires agents to integrate supporting evidence across multiple historical events or transfer preferences inferred in one app to decisions in another. Success therefore requires reasoning about the user rather than simply retrieving a single past event. Real-world personalization can be even more complex, as things can diverge from past trends and historical behavior cannot be treated as unconditional specification of future intent. Therefore, we introduce three perturbation types: (1) Instruction perturbation : The current user instruction explicitly contradicts the dominant historical pattern. For example, a user who typically selects an inexpensive tier for rideshare may explicitly ask for a premium ride for a special trip. The agent must prioritize the current instruction over an inferred historical preference. (2) Preference perturbation : Recent behavior in ℋ \mathcal{H} suggests that the user’s preference has shifted over time and departed from the long-run mode. For example, the user selected aisle seats consistently in recent months, while most historical flights were window seats. A personalized agent should therefore identify the evolving preference trend, rather than simply selecting the most frequent historical value. (3) Environment perturbation : The preferred option becomes unavailable in the current environment. The agent should respond to the situation by recognizing the unavailability, surfacing it to the user, and acting according to the user’s preference for alternatives or stopping if no substitution is acceptable. Task Authoring and Quality Assurance. We use a three-stage task authoring and validation pipeline to ensure realistic underspecification, task feasibility, grounded resolution for each omitted requirement, and verifiable outcomes. First, coding agents with task-authoring skills generate candidate personalized tasks using the source code of the apps, user activity history and profile, and fully specified iOSWorld tasks as references. Second, human task-refinement experts review and revise each candidate task. Specifically, for each omitted detail, experts verify its resolution source. An inferable detail must be supported by a dominant pattern or explicit fact in ℋ \mathcal{H} , and where the evidence is weak or mixed, we revise the seeded data so that ℋ \mathcal{H} can support a clear preference sufficiently. An ask-only detail must not be recoverable from ℋ \mathcal{H} , and its intended value is chosen to differ from the app’s pre-filled default when possible, so that silently accepting a default or guessing is unlikely to succeed by chance. At this stage, experts also remove duplicate tasks and diversify the candidate tasks to cover as many user preferences and apps as possible. Finally, experienced validation experts execute refined tasks in the simulator to verify environmental feasibility and rubric correctness, and correct remaining issues accordingly. Every task in the final iPrefBench therefore undergoes two rounds of human review and revision. More details are provided in Appendix D.1 . 3.4 Evaluation A personalized agent should complete user requests successfully with appropriate personalization, asking the user for additional information only when necessary. There are multiple failure modes: it may execute the correct operation while making wrong user-dependent choices (e.g., purchasing a game controller as requested, but not the model compatible with the user’s console), or eventually reach the correct outcome by repeatedly asking the user for every detail. We therefore evaluate two aspects of agent behavior: (1) Personalized Task Completion, for whether the agent completes the required operations and whether it personalizes them for the user correctly; and (2) User-Agent Interaction, for whether it involves the user only when necessary. More details are provided in Appendix E . Personalized Task Completion. Each task is accompanied by a task-specific rubric containing two types of criteria. Each action-completion criterion evaluates an operation required by the instruction, independent of user-specific choices. For instance, a criterion requires that the agent successfully creates a restaurant reservation, regardless of the restaurant, time, or party size. Each personalization criterion corresponds to a user-dependent decision involved in the task, and is additionally labeled with its resolution source (i.e., inferable or ask-only). For example, correctly reserving the user’s usual restaurant satisfies an inferable personalization criterion, and reserving at the intended time and party size satisfies the ask-only personalization criteria. An LLM judge ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) evaluates each criterion as pass or fail using the execution trajectory (including screenshots, actions, and the final answer), user profile, task-specific hidden context, and rubric. Action-completion and personalization scores are computed as the fractions of satisfied criteria in their corresponding category, macro-averaged over tasks. A task counts as a success only if all of its criteria are satisfied. User-Agent Interaction. Following the cooperative principle in conversation that a contribution should be as informative as required, and no more ( Grice et al., 1975 ) , we evaluate whether agents request all ask-only information while avoiding unnecessary questions. We first use an LLM judge to decompose ask_user messages from the agent into a multiset of individual information requests 𝒬 t \mathcal{Q}_{t} . Multiple independent requests within one message are treated separately, and repeated requests are counted as separate occurrences. Each request q ∈ 𝒬 t q\in\mathcal{Q}_{t} is semantically matched to an ask-only requirement, if any: ϕ t ​ ( q ) ∈ U t ask ∪ { ⊥ } \phi_{t}(q)\in U_{t}^{\mathrm{ask}}\cup\{\bot\} , where ⊥ \bot denotes no match. The set of distinct ask-only requirements elicited by the agent is E t = { u ∈ U t ask | ∃ q ∈ 𝒬 t , ϕ t ( q ) = u } . E_{t}=\left\{u\in U_{t}^{\mathrm{ask}}\;\middle|\;\exists q\in\mathcal{Q}_{t},\ \phi_{t}(q)=u\right\}. We then compute interaction Recall and Precision as Recall = ∑ t | E t | / ∑ t | U t a ​ s ​ k | \text{Recall}=\sum_{t}|E_{t}|/\sum_{t}|U^{ask}_{t}| and Precision = ∑ t | E t | / ∑ t | Q t | \text{Precision}=\sum_{t}|E_{t}|/\sum_{t}|Q_{t}| . Recall measures the fraction of ask-only details the agent elicits, while Precision measures the fraction of request occurrences that cover a new ask-only requirement, penalizing requests for inferable or irrelevant information as well as repeated requests. Together, these metrics penalize both agents that silently fabricate what they cannot know and those that excessively burden the user with exhaustive questions. 3.5 Benchmark Statistics The resulting iPrefBench contains 130 130 tasks, grounded in 3 , 051 3,051 user activity events across 26 26 apps. We center on two core capabilities for personalized agents: inferring user preferences from the user’s activity history, and asking the user for clarification when necessary. For each underspecified task, the agent needs to determine not only which information is missing, but also where it should come from. By controlling the provenance of each omitted detail, iPrefBench enables evaluation of whether the agent can execute the required action (i.e., action completion) and complete the task correctly for the particular user (i.e., personalization), and whether it involves the user only when necessary (i.e., user-agent interaction). Our evaluation on seven frontier agents reveals a clear gap between action execution and personalization, especially when the user preferences can only be obtained by asking. Agents struggle most to recognize which information is genuinely unavailable and requires user input. Explicitly encouraging clarification increases the number of questions, but at the cost of over-asking. These findings suggest that we are still far from a truly personalized agent that can know what to infer and when to ask. B.3 Per-Task Environment Control All tasks in iPrefBench share a single seeded environment and base activity history ℋ \mathcal{H} . However, some tasks, particularly the perturbation tasks (§ 3.3 ), require the environment to differ from this shared seed. iPrefBench supports a small set of declarative per-task fields, which are applied at episode setup and reverted afterwards: 1. Data overrides patch the data served by an app for the current task, e.g., marking an item out of stock, clearing a restaurant’s availability, or extending an app’s in-app history. 2. Log events append synthetic activity events to the history ℋ \mathcal{H} rendered for the current task only. 3. Profile overrides update entries of the user profile 𝒫 \mathcal{P} used by the simulator and the judges, for tasks where the user’s present preference diverges from the historical pattern. For example, environment perturbations are implemented through data overrides, while preference perturbations require log events to change the agent-received user activity history, data overrides to make sure the on-screen app data is consistent, and profile overrides to reflect the updated preference for the user simulator and evaluators. Appendix C User Details Following iOSWorld ( Jang et al., 2026 ) , all applications in the simulator are seeded with data around a single fictional persona, Jordan Avery . iPrefBench exposes information about this user to the agent in two ways: (1) a chronological user activity history ℋ \mathcal{H} , provided to the agent as prior context (Appendix C.1 ), and (2) an interactive user simulator that the agent can consult through ask_user (Appendix C.3 ). The simulator is grounded in a structured user profile 𝒫 \mathcal{P} derived from the seeded data (Appendix C.2 ), which also serves as ground truth for evaluation but is never shown to the agent. C.1 User Activity History We construct the user activity history ℋ \mathcal{H} by converting the seeded application data into a unified, chronological sequence of natural-language events. Each event is represented by its timestamp followed by a natural-language description of the activity, which is converted from its metadata with an LLM (Claude Sonnet 5). Events are ordered chronologically, preserving temporal information that may be important for inferring recurring habits and evolving preferences. The following are two example events from the activity history: [2025-08-01 16:55] in MyBank transferred $300.00 from Total Checking to Savings for monthly savings. [2026-02-19 02:06] in QuickChat received a message from Camille Hart in Brunch Crew: “Alright, making this group official. Monthly brunch is non-negotiable.” By combining activities from different applications into a single history, ℋ \mathcal{H} allows agents to infer user information beyond the context of any individual application. For example, payment transactions, restaurant orders, and restaurant ratings may jointly provide evidence of dining preferences, and messages and travel bookings may provide complementary information about travel plans. The activity history ℋ \mathcal{H} is provided to the agent as its only prior knowledge of the user. In the default evaluation setting, the agent receives the full history at the beginning of each task. All inferable requirements in iPrefBench are grounded in evidence available in H H . In contrast, ask-only requirements cannot be resolved from the history and must be obtained through the ask_user action. C.2 User Profile We derive a structured user profile 𝒫 \mathcal{P} for the persona, grounded in the seeded application data and the corresponding user activity history ℋ \mathcal{H} . The profile captures the user’s identity, relationships, preferences, habits, and other personal information across 13 13 dimensions, comprising 92 92 entries in total. Each entry records its value together with an evidence field that points to the supporting events in ℋ \mathcal{H} , and every piece of information in 𝒫 \mathcal{P} is designed to be recoverable from the history. Profile entries are first extracted with coding agents from the seeded data in ℋ \mathcal{H} , and manually verified against their evidence in ℋ \mathcal{H} during the task-authoring process. The structured profile serves as a hidden oracle for the user simulator and evaluation. It is not directly exposed to the agent under test. C.4 Human Validation of User Simulator We manually annotate all agent-user interactions produced by four representative agents in our experiments (Claude Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.7 Flash, Kimi K3, Qwen3.8-27B), yielding 89 89 question-answer pairs. For each question-answer pair, we check it in two aspects: • Grounding: Whether every fact in the reply is supported by the user profile, hidden task context, or the reply honestly declines something the profile genuinely does not cover. Fabricated (i.e., the reply states a concrete detail that appears nowhere in the profile or context), Contradicts (i.e., the reply gives a value that conflicts with the profile or task context), Wrongly withheld (i.e., the reply claims not to know, or refuses, when the answer is in fact available) and Can’t tell (i.e., the profile is ambiguous or the question is too vague to judge) are all counted as failures. • Scope: Whether the reply answers everything asked and nothing more. Volunteered extra (i.e., the reply adds information the agent did not request) and Incomplete (i.e., the reply leaves part of the question unanswered) are all counted as failures. 96.6 96.6 % of pairs (86 of 89) are valid on both axes. Both grounding failures occur in tasks without ask-only requirements, where the simulator has no direct answer and must improvise for agent-produced unnecessary questions. The single scope failure is a reservation task in which the agent asks three specific questions (date, party size, and restaurant) and the simulator answers all three but additionally supplies the time. Appendix D Task Details D.1 Task Collection We construct iPrefBench through a three-stage pipeline consisting of automated candidate generation, human refinement, and execution-based validation. The pipeline produces 188 188 initial candidate tasks, from which 130 130 tasks are retained in the final benchmark. Stage 1: Automated Candidate Generation. We develop two task-authoring skills for coding agents to generate candidate tasks. The first skill generates personalized mobile-use tasks using the application source code, seeded user data, user activity history, structured user profile, and fully specified tasks from iOSWorld as references. Candidate tasks are designed to resemble realistic user requests while leaving user-dependent information underspecified. The second skill focuses on generating tasks with three types of perturbations: instruction perturbations, preference perturbations, and environment perturbations. These tasks introduce cases in which an explicit instruction overrides historical behavior, recent evidence indicates a change in preference, or a preferred option becomes unavailable in the environment. Together, the two skills generate an initial pool of 188 candidate tasks. Stage 2: Human Refinement. Eight human reviewers refine the generated candidates. They review the naturalness of each user instruction, verify that the requested operations are feasible in the environment, and identify the user-dependent information omitted from the instruction. For each omitted requirement, reviewers determine its resolution source and ensure that it is well grounded. An inferable requirement must be supported by a dominant pattern or an explicit fact in ℋ \mathcal{H} ; when the supporting evidence is weak or mixed, reviewers revise the seeded data so that ℋ \mathcal{H} supports a clear preference. An ask-only requirement must not be recoverable from ℋ \mathcal{H} , and its intended value is specified in the task-specific hidden context. Whenever possible, this value is chosen to differ from the app’s pre-filled default, so that silently accepting the default or guessing is unlikely to succeed by chance. Reviewers revise ambiguous requirements and the corresponding task rubrics to ensure that each requirement has a well-defined ground-truth value and resolution source. For tasks whose conditions must diverge from the shared environment, such as perturbation tasks, reviewers also specify or revise the corresponding per-task overrides (Appendix B.3 ). The reviewers also remove duplicate tasks and refine the candidate pool to improve coverage of different applications, user preferences, and task scenarios. Stage 3: Execution-Based Validation. Two experienced human validators execute the refined tasks in the iOS simulator. This stage checks that the requested operations can be completed in the environment and that the task rubrics correctly specify the expected outcomes. Remaining issues in task instructions, environmental feasibility, and rubrics are corrected during validation. Following refinement and validation, we retain 130 130 tasks in the final benchmark. Each retained task undergoes both human refinement and execution-based validation. Appendix E Rubric and Interaction Judge Details E.1 Task-specific Rubrics Each task is associated with a rubric containing two types of criteria: action-completion and personalization criteria. Action-completion criteria specify the operations required to complete the task, independently of the values selected for user-dependent parameters. Personalization criteria assess whether the agent makes the correct user-dependent decisions. Each personalization criterion is additionally annotated with its information resolution source: inferable , if the intended value can be recovered from the user activity history ℋ \mathcal{H} , or ask-only , if the value is unavailable in ℋ \mathcal{H} and must be obtained through user interaction. E.2 Rubric-Based Completion Judge We use an LLM-based judge (with Claude Sonnet 5) to evaluate each rubric criterion independently. The judge receives the task instruction, the complete execution trajectory, and the agent’s final answer. The trajectory contains the executed actions and screenshots at each step, together with a screenshot of the final interface state. The judge additionally receives the ground-truth user profile and task-specific hidden context when applicable. The judge is also given the run time of the task, i.e., the simulator clock during execution, to resolve relative temporal expressions such as “tomorrow” or “next Saturday.” For each criterion, the judge returns a binary label and a supporting explanation. A criterion passes only when the trajectory provides clear evidence that it has been satisfied. We compute action-completion and personalization scores as the fractions of satisfied criteria within their respective categories. Both action-completion and personalization scores are macro-averaged across tasks. Personalization is further reported separately for inferable and ask-only criteria, which are macro-aggregated over tasks containing at least one criterion of the corresponding type. A task is considered fully successful only if all of its action-completion and personalization criteria are satisfied. E.3 Interaction Judge To evaluate whether agents ask appropriate clarification questions, we analyze the ask_user messages produced during each task. The interaction judge receives all clarification questions issued during a task and the task’s annotated set of ask-only information. It identifies the individual pieces of information requested by the agent and semantically matches each piece to an ask-only requirement, if applicable. One information piece corresponds to a single decision or value the user must supply. A question requesting several independent values is decomposed into multiple pieces. Conversely, a question offering several candidate answers for the same decision is counted as a single piece. Repeated requests are counted separately, even when they concern the same information. For each extracted piece, the judge returns a short description and either the matched ask-only requirement or a null match. Matching is semantic rather than based on exact wording. Requests for information that is inferable from history, irrelevant to the task, or otherwise not among the ask-only requirements receive null matches. Both interaction Recall and Precision are micro-aggregated: we sum the number of distinct ask-only requirements elicited, the total number of ask-only requirements, and the total number of information requests across all tasks. Format-Level Message Quality. We also examine the format-level quality of each agent message along three criteria: specificity (i.e., it is clear which piece of information is being requested) ( Vijayvargiya et al., 2026 ) , answerability (i.e., the user can answer from knowledge they plausibly have, given the context the message supplies) ( Vijayvargiya et al., 2026 ) , and option provision (i.e., when the answer space is a small closed set, the message surfaces the candidates rather than leaving the user to enumerate them) ( Peng et al., 2025 ) . An LLM judge scores each criterion on every message issued by the agent whenever the criterion applies, and the overall quality score is the message-level average over the applicable criteria.
